events.title: Earliest Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows earliest human activity in present-day Argentina dates to around 11000 BCE. In Patagonia's Cueva de las Manos (Cave of Hands), ancient hunter-gatherers left handprint paintings. These early inhabitants hunted large animals like guanacos and llamas, developing survival skills adapted to different geographic environments.

events.title: Agricultural Development
events.description: In northwestern Argentina's Andean region, indigenous peoples began developing agriculture, cultivating corn, squash and beans. They domesticated llamas and alpacas for transport and wool. This period marked transition from nomadic hunter-gathering to settled agricultural societies.

events.title: Regional Cultural Development
events.description: Different regions of Argentina developed distinct indigenous cultures. Northwest influenced by Andean highland cultures, central plains developed hunting cultures, southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego had maritime hunter-gatherer cultures. These cultural groups included Diaguita, Guaraní, Mapuche, Quechua and others.

events.title: Inca Empire Expansion
events.description: Inca Empire under Tupac Inca Yupanqui expanded southward, conquering present-day northwestern Argentina. Incas built road systems, fortresses and administrative centers, integrating these regions into empire's economic and political system. Local Diaguita and other tribes were incorporated into Inca rule but retained partial autonomy. Inca rule introduced Quechua language, advanced agricultural techniques and religious rituals.

events.title: First European Arrival
events.description: Spanish explorer Juan Díaz de Solís first reached Río de la Plata, becoming first European to reach present-day Argentina. Solís was killed in conflict with local Charrúa tribe. Though expedition ended tragically, this contact opened Spanish interest in La Plata region.

events.title: First Buenos Aires Foundation
events.description: Spanish conquistador Pedro de Mendoza first founded Buenos Aires city on Río de la Plata banks. However, due to starvation, disease and continuous indigenous attacks, settlement could not sustain. In 1541, survivors forced to abandon city for Asunción. This failed attempt showed difficulty of establishing permanent colony in region.

events.title: Northwestern Colonization
events.description: Spanish colonists from Peru began entering northwestern Argentina from north, establishing series of cities. These included Santiago del Estero (1553), Córdoba (1573) and Salta (1582). These settlements became important nodes connecting Viceroyalty of Peru with La Plata region.

events.title: Permanent Buenos Aires Foundation
events.description: Juan de Garay led expedition from Asunción to re-establish Buenos Aires city, naming it 'City of the Holy Trinity and Port of Saint Mary of the Fair Winds.' This foundation was permanent, city gradually developed into major port of La Plata region. Though initially sparsely populated with limited economy, Buenos Aires' strategic location enabled continuous growth over following centuries.

events.title: Jesuit Missions
events.description: Jesuits established series of missions (reduciones) in present-day northern Argentina, Paraguay and Brazil border regions, protecting Guaraní indigenous from slave traders. These missions became self-sufficient communities, developing agriculture, handicrafts and music. Missions represented unique social experiment, blending Catholic faith with indigenous culture. Most famous included San Ignacio Miní and Santa Ana missions.

events.title: Jesuit Expulsion
events.description: Spanish King Charles III ordered Jesuits expelled from all Spanish territories, including La Plata region. Thousands of Jesuits were forced to leave, their missions taken over by secular authorities. This led to collapse of mission system, many Guaraní displaced. This event had profound impact on region's social and economic structure.

events.title: Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata Established
events.description: Spanish King Charles III created Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata with Buenos Aires as capital, separating from Viceroyalty of Peru. New viceroyalty included present-day Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. This administrative reform reflected Buenos Aires' growing economic importance and aimed to better manage and defend region, especially against Portuguese expansion in Brazil.

events.title: British Invasions
events.description: British forces twice attempted to occupy Buenos Aires but were repelled by local militias. These events called 'British Invasions' saw defense led by local Criollos (Spanish descendants born in Americas) without major Spanish military support. Successful resistance boosted Criollo confidence and national consciousness, planting seeds for future independence movement. Leaders like Santiago de Liniers and Juan Martín de Pueyrredón became heroes.

events.title: May Revolution
events.description: Buenos Aires Criollo elite, learning of Spain's occupation by Napoleon, staged coup overthrowing viceroy, establishing first local government - Primera Junta. This event marked beginning of Argentina's independence process, now considered national independence day. Revolutionary leaders included Cornelio Saavedra, Manuel Belgrano and Mariano Moreno. Though revolution nominally claimed loyalty to imprisoned Spanish King Ferdinand VII, it actually opened path to complete independence.

events.title: Flag and Anthem Birth
events.description: General Manuel Belgrano created Argentine flag, adopting sky blue and white colors. Same year, Vicente López y Planes composed Argentine national anthem. Creation of these national symbols reflected formation of emerging national identity, though complete independence not yet formally declared.

events.title: Declaration of Independence
events.description: Congress of Tucumán formally declared independence of United Provinces of La Plata from Spain. This historic declaration signed by representatives from various provinces, establishing Argentina's status as sovereign nation. Declaration made in context of General José de San Martín leading Army of Andes across mountains to liberate Chile and Peru.

events.title: San Martín's Liberation Wars
events.description: General José de San Martín led Army of Andes across Andes Mountains, defeating Spanish forces in Battles of Chacabuco (1817) and Maipú (1818), liberating Chile. Subsequently, he led expedition to Peru, occupying Lima in 1821 and declaring Peruvian independence. After Guayaquil meeting with Simón Bolívar in 1822, San Martín chose to withdraw from political arena, but his military achievements made him key figure in South American independence and Argentine national hero.

events.title: Period of Anarchy
events.description: After independence, Argentina fell into civil war and political chaos, called 'Period of Anarchy.' Conflict between Centralists (Unitarios) and Federalists led to violence and political instability. Disputes between Buenos Aires and interior provinces over trade, tariffs and political power divided nation. This period saw rise of numerous caudillos (warlords), each controlling different regions.

events.title: Rosas Dictatorship
events.description: Juan Manuel de Rosas came to power as Buenos Aires governor, implementing 23-year authoritarian rule. Rosas was Federalist leader but practiced centralized rule, brutally suppressing opposition, establishing secret police (Mazorca). He controlled foreign trade, maintained alliances with interior provinces. Rosas' rule brought stability but at high cost, restricting freedoms and causing many intellectuals to exile, including future leaders like Domingo Sarmiento and Juan Bautista Alberdi.

events.title: Battle of Caseros
events.description: General Justo José de Urquiza, governor of Entre Ríos, led coalition forces defeating Rosas at Battle of Caseros, ending his rule. Rosas exiled to Britain, never returning to Argentina. This battle opened path for national organization and constitutional formation. Urquiza became leader of new government, but tensions between Buenos Aires and other provinces remained.

events.title: Constitution Adopted
events.description: Constitutional Convention in Santa Fe adopted Argentine Constitution, establishing federal republican system, modeled on US Constitution. Constitution specified separation of powers, federalism and civil rights. However, Buenos Aires refused to join federation, becoming independent state for decade. Constitution mainly influenced by Juan Bautista Alberdi's ideas, advocating immigration, education and economic modernization.

events.title: National Unification
events.description: Buenos Aires forces led by Bartolomé Mitre defeated federal forces at Battle of Pavón, finally achieving national unification. Buenos Aires joined Argentine federation, constitution revised to accommodate Buenos Aires' entry. Mitre became first president of unified nation (1862-1868), opening period of nation-building and modernization.

events.title: War of the Triple Alliance
events.description: Argentina allied with Brazil and Uruguay against Paraguay. This bloody conflict was one of deadliest wars in South American history, causing massive Paraguayan population loss. War triggered by Paraguayan dictator Francisco Solano López's expansionism. Though Argentina won and gained territory, war drained national resources, caused thousands of Argentine soldier deaths, and intensified political divisions.

events.title: Sarmiento Presidency
events.description: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento served as president, promoting education and cultural development. Sarmiento established thousands of schools, founded teacher training colleges, promoted public education. His motto 'Civilization and Barbarism' reflected his vision of bringing European-style modernization to Argentina, though this view held negative attitudes toward indigenous and gaucho culture. Sarmiento's reforms laid foundation for Argentine education system.

events.title: Conquest of the Desert
events.description: General Julio Argentino Roca led military campaign conquering Patagonia and Pampas, euphemistically called 'Conquest of the Desert.' Campaign was actually genocidal war against region's indigenous peoples (Mapuche, Ranquel, etc.), causing thousands of deaths, survivors forcibly relocated or enslaved. Campaign opened vast fertile lands for Argentina, distributed to European immigrants and influential landowners. Roca became president as result, but campaign remains one of Argentina's most controversial events.

events.title: Buenos Aires Federalization
events.description: After intense political struggle and even brief armed conflict, Buenos Aires city was federalized, becoming Argentina's official capital. Buenos Aires province established new capital at La Plata. This decision ended long power struggle between Buenos Aires and other provinces, consolidating national unity.

events.title: Conservative Regime Period
events.description: Argentina ruled by conservative elite oligarchy, period called 'Infamous Decade' (actually lasted 36 years). Ruling class maintained power through electoral fraud and restricted suffrage. Despite political corruption, period witnessed unprecedented economic growth, massive immigration and infrastructure development. Argentina became major world exporter of grain and beef, Buenos Aires developed into thriving international metropolis.

events.title: Great Immigration Wave
events.description: Millions of European immigrants, mainly from Italy and Spain, flooded Argentina seeking better life. Immigration estimated at 6 million, completely transforming Argentina's demographics, culture and society. Immigrants brought new skills, ideas and traditions, including socialist and anarchist ideas. They settled in cities working in industry and services, or in countryside becoming farmers. This period's immigration shaped modern Argentina's multicultural character.

events.title: Civic Union Established
events.description: Reformist politicians established Civic Union (later Radical Civic Union, UCR), opposing conservative regime's electoral fraud and corruption. Leaders Leandro Alem and Hipólito Yrigoyen demanded electoral reform, expanded suffrage and democratization. Radical Party became main opposition force, representing emerging middle class interests.

events.title: Revolution of 1890
events.description: Armed uprising led by Radical Civic Union attempted to overthrow President Julio Roca's government. Though uprising failed, it exposed political system's fragility and forced President Miguel Juárez Celman to resign. This event marked strengthening of political movement opposing conservative oligarchy, paving way for future reforms.

events.title: Sáenz Peña Electoral Law
events.description: President Roque Sáenz Peña promoted electoral reform law stipulating universal male suffrage, secret ballot and mandatory voting. This law ended era of conservative elite monopolizing power through electoral fraud, opening door for Radical Party and other political forces to compete. This was major milestone in Argentina's democratization.

events.title: WWI Neutrality
events.description: Argentina maintained neutrality during WWI, despite pressure from Allies to enter war. Neutrality enabled Argentina to supply food and meat to both sides, bringing huge economic benefits. After war ended, Argentina was among world's wealthiest nations, with per capita income among global leaders.

events.title: Yrigoyen Elected President
events.description: Radical Civic Union's Hipólito Yrigoyen elected president in first truly free election, ending conservative oligarchy rule. Yrigoyen represented middle and working class interests, promoting social reforms, expanding state role in economy, supporting labor rights. His election marked turning point in Argentine politics, opening era of broader political participation.

events.title: University Reform Movement
events.description: University of Córdoba students launched reform movement demanding university autonomy, student participation in governance, academic freedom and modernized curriculum. Movement quickly spread throughout Latin America, becoming paradigm for student radicalism. Argentine government eventually accepted reform demands, completely transforming higher education system, making it more democratic and progressive.

events.title: Tragic Week
events.description: Massive worker strike in Buenos Aires brutally suppressed by police and military, causing hundreds of deaths, known as 'Tragic Week.' Repression accompanied by violence against Jewish community, falsely accused of inciting strike. This event showed intensifying social tensions and conflict between labor movement and government.

events.title: Infamous Decade
events.description: Conservative forces regained power through electoral fraud (so-called 'patriotic fraud'), suppressing Radical Party and leftist forces. This period economy severely affected by Great Depression, unemployment and social inequality intensified. Nevertheless, Argentina began industrialization process, reducing dependence on agricultural exports. Political corruption and undemocratic practices caused public to lose faith in traditional parties.

events.title: First Military Coup
events.description: General José Félix Uriburu led military coup overthrowing elected President Hipólito Yrigoyen, opening Argentina's 'Infamous Decade' and era of military intervention in politics. Coup supported by conservative elite and middle class fearful of social unrest. This coup set precedent for Argentine military overthrowing elected governments, recurring over next 50 years.

events.title: 1943 Military Coup
events.description: Group of nationalist officers staged coup overthrowing President Ramón Castillo's conservative government. Coup organized by United Officers Group (GOU), members including Colonel Juan Domingo Perón. New military government promoted nationalist policies, remained neutral in WWII, strengthened state control of economy. Perón served as Labor Minister in government, beginning to build his alliance with working class.

events.title: Peronism Birth
events.description: Juan Perón arrested by opponents within military government, but working class launched massive demonstrations demanding his release. Hundreds of thousands of workers flooded Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo, forcing military government to release Perón. This day became Peronism movement's birthday, symbolizing strong political alliance between Perón and working class. Perón's relationship with actress Evita Duarte (later Eva Perón) also became public during this period.

events.title: Perón Elected President
events.description: Juan Domingo Perón elected president with overwhelming majority in democratic election, supported by workers, unions and military. Perón promoted populist policies including worker rights, social welfare, industrialization and economic nationalism. He established 'Justicialist Party' (Peronist Party), becoming dominant force in Argentine politics. Perón's first lady Eva Perón (Evita) played key role in promoting social programs and winning popular support.

events.title: Women's Suffrage
events.description: With Eva Perón's strong advocacy, Argentina passed law granting women's suffrage. This was major victory for women's rights movement in Latin America. In 1951, women first participated in presidential election voting. Eva Perón herself became symbol of women's rights and social justice, deeply loved by lower classes, called 'Spiritual Leader of the Poor.'

events.title: New Constitution
events.description: Perón government promulgated new constitution allowing presidential re-election, expanding labor rights and social security, nationalizing some key industries. New constitution reflected Peronism's 'Third Position' ideology - neither capitalism nor communism, but Argentine path of social justice and economic independence. Constitution strengthened presidential power, weakened checks and balances.

events.title: Eva Perón's Death
events.description: Eva Perón (Evita) died of cervical cancer at age 33. Her death triggered national mourning, millions attended funeral. During life, Evita helped poor through her charitable foundation, promoted women's rights, becoming one of most charismatic figures in Argentine history. Her early death became turning point for Perón regime's decline, also making her immortal legendary figure.

events.title: Peronism Banned Period
events.description: After Perón overthrown, Peronism banned in Argentina for 18 years. Nevertheless, Peronist Party remained most popular political force, Perón continued to influence Argentine politics from exile. This period witnessed alternation between military and civilian governments, political instability, economic decline. Peronists went underground, organizing resistance movements, including left-wing Peronists who later evolved into guerrillas.

events.title: Liberating Revolution
events.description: Military coup overthrew President Perón, called 'Liberating Revolution.' Anti-Peronist officers, conservatives and Catholic Church united to overthrow Perón, accusing him of dictatorship, corruption and economic destruction. Perón exiled to Spain for 18 years. New military government banned Peronism, persecuted Peronist supporters, even prohibited mentioning Perón or Evita's names. This opened one of most turbulent periods in Argentine history.

events.title: Frondizi Presidency
events.description: Radical Party's Arturo Frondizi elected president after secret agreement with Perón. Frondizi attempted to promote economic developmentalism, attract foreign investment, develop industry. But he faced continuous military pressure and political instability. In 1962, after allowing Peronists to participate in elections, military staged coup overthrowing him.

events.title: Argentine Revolution Military Government
events.description: General Juan Carlos Onganía led military coup establishing authoritarian military government, called 'Argentine Revolution.' Military government suppressed political activity, censored media, intervened in universities. Economic policies initially brought growth but later stagnated. Authoritarian rule and social restrictions triggered widespread protests, especially 1969's Cordobazo, marking military government's authority decline.

events.title: Cordobazo
events.description: Córdoba city erupted in massive worker and student uprising against military government's authoritarian rule and economic policies. Protests evolved into violent clashes, demonstrators controlled city for days. This uprising shocked military government, marking climax of 1960s social protests. Cordobazo inspired similar protests in other cities and prompted emergence of left-wing guerrilla organizations.

events.title: Left-Wing Guerrilla Movements
events.description: Several left-wing guerrilla organizations emerged, including Montoneros (left-wing Peronists) and People's Revolutionary Army (ERP, Trotskyist). These organizations conducted kidnappings, assassinations and armed attacks, aiming to overthrow military government and establish socialist revolution. Most famous operation included 1970 kidnapping and execution of former president Aramburu. Guerrilla activity reflected Cold War era wave of revolutionary movements in Latin America.

events.title: Perón's Return and Third Presidency
events.description: After military government agreed to open elections, Peronists won. Perón initially not allowed to run, but his proxy resigned after election, paving way for Perón's return and new election. In 1973, 78-year-old Perón returned to Argentina, welcomed by millions of supporters. He was elected president third time, third wife Isabel Perón as vice president. But Perón faced split between left and right-wing Peronists, economic crisis and escalating violence.

events.title: Ezeiza Massacre
events.description: Day Perón returned from exile to Argentina, near Ezeiza airport, violent clashes erupted between right and left-wing Peronists. Right-wing Peronist militia opened fire on left-wing Montoneros supporters, causing at least 13 deaths, hundreds injured. This event exposed deep divisions within Peronism movement, foreshadowing future violent conflicts. Perón himself increasingly leaned rightward, breaking with left-wing guerrillas.

events.title: Perón's Death and Isabel's Succession
events.description: Juan Domingo Perón died of heart attack at age 78. His third wife Isabel Perón succeeded, becoming world's first female president. However, Isabel lacked political experience and authority, unable to control worsening economic crisis and political violence. Her government influenced by right-wing death squads (Argentine Anticommunist Alliance, AAA), which assassinated left-wing activists and intellectuals.

events.title: Political Violence Escalation
events.description: Argentina plunged into severe political violence, conflicts between left-wing guerrillas, right-wing death squads and security forces causing daily casualties. Economy collapsed, inflation soared, society fell into chaos. Isabel Perón government completely lost control, military prepared to intervene. This period's chaos created conditions for coming military coup and military dictatorship.

events.title: Dirty War
events.description: Military government conducted systematic state terrorism, approximately 30,000 people disappeared or killed, called 'disappeared' (desaparecidos). Victims secretly kidnapped, held in secret detention centers, tortured, then killed, bodies disposed or secretly buried. Many victims were young people, students, union members, journalists and social activists, many unrelated to guerrilla activity. Military government also stole babies from political prisoners, giving them to military families for adoption. This reign of terror was one of most severe human rights violations in Latin America during Cold War, supported by US under 'Operation Condor' framework.

events.title: Military Coup and National Reorganization Process
events.description: Military staged coup overthrowing Isabel Perón, establishing military government called 'National Reorganization Process' (Proceso de Reorganización Nacional). Military government led by General Jorge Rafael Videla promised to restore order and combat subversion. But military government soon began systematic state terrorism, kidnapping, torturing and murdering left-wing activists, students, union members and anyone deemed threatening. This opened Argentina's darkest period - the Dirty War.

events.title: Mothers of Plaza de Mayo Movement
events.description: Mothers of disappeared began weekly Thursday marches in Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo, wearing white headscarves, holding photos of disappeared children, demanding to know their whereabouts. These brave women openly challenged military government during reign of terror, becoming symbol of human rights movement. Mothers of Plaza de Mayo organization became world-famous human rights organization, their struggle continues today demanding truth and justice.

events.title: World Cup Football
events.description: Argentina hosted and won World Cup football, defeating Netherlands in final. Military government used World Cup as propaganda tool, displaying 'normal' and 'orderly' Argentina, covering up ongoing human rights violations. World Cup victory brought brief national unity and support for military government, but critics pointed out this whitewashed reign of terror. Many human rights organizations protested hosting World Cup under dictatorship.

events.title: Economic Crisis
events.description: Military government's neoliberal economic policies led to severe crisis. Economic Minister José Martínez de Hoz's policies caused de-industrialization, debt surge and economic collapse. Argentina's foreign debt increased from $8 billion in 1976 to $45 billion in 1983. Unemployment and poverty rose sharply, public support for military government disappeared. Economic disaster further damaged military government's legitimacy.

events.title: Malvinas/Falklands War
events.description: Military government leader General Leopoldo Galtieri invaded Malvinas Islands (British call Falkland Islands), attempting to save military government's prestige through nationalism. Argentina claimed sovereignty over these islands controlled by Britain since 19th century. Initially, invasion triggered patriotic fervor in Argentina, but Britain under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher sent task force to reclaim islands. After 74-day war, Argentine forces surrendered, causing about 650 Argentine soldier deaths. Defeat completely destroyed military government's prestige, accelerating its collapse.

events.title: Democratic Elections
events.description: After Malvinas defeat, military government forced to hold democratic elections. Radical Civic Union's Raúl Alfonsín defeated Peronist candidate, elected president. This was Argentina's first free election since 1973, marking democracy's restoration. Alfonsín promised to prosecute military for human rights crimes, rebuild democratic institutions, restore economy.

events.title: Democracy Restored
events.description: Raúl Alfonsín sworn in as president, ending seven-year military dictatorship, restoring constitutional democracy. Alfonsín's inaugural speech emphasized human rights, rule of law and democratic values, hundreds of thousands celebrated in Buenos Aires streets. Democracy's restoration symbolic not only for Argentina but entire South America, as region transitioned from military dictatorships to democracy.

events.title: CONADEP Report
events.description: National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP) established by President Alfonsín released report 'Nunca Más' (Never Again), documenting human rights violations during military dictatorship. Report confirmed nearly 9,000 disappearance cases (actual number possibly near 30,000), detailed torture centers, secret detention and murder. Report became important part of Argentine and global human rights documentation, providing basis for prosecuting crimes.

events.title: Junta Trials
events.description: Argentina conducted historic trials of military government leaders, nine former military government members tried. Jorge Videla and Emilio Massera sentenced to life imprisonment, others also convicted. Trials held publicly, survivors testified, exposing Dirty War horrors. This was first time in Latin America democratic government tried former military dictators, setting precedent for transitional justice in region.

events.title: Military Rebellions and Amnesty Laws
events.description: Facing military resistance to trials and several military rebellions, Alfonsín government forced to pass 'Full Stop Law' and 'Due Obedience Law,' limiting prosecution of lower-ranking officers. These laws essentially gave most military participants in Dirty War protection from prosecution. Human rights organizations strongly opposed these laws, viewing them as betrayal of justice, but Alfonsín believed they necessary to maintain democratic stability.

events.title: Hyperinflation Crisis
events.description: Argentine economy collapsed, annual inflation rate reaching nearly 5000%, causing hyperinflation. Currency devalued, prices rising daily, people's savings destroyed. Supermarket looting occurred, society fell into chaos. Economic crisis forced President Alfonsín to transfer power six months early to elected President Carlos Menem. This was Argentina's first peaceful democratic power transfer since 1928, but conducted amid crisis.

events.title: Menem Presidency and Neoliberal Reforms
events.description: Peronist Party's Carlos Menem as president promoted radical neoliberal economic reforms, sharply contrasting with traditional Peronism's statist policies. Reforms included massive privatization (telecommunications, oil, aviation, etc.), market opening, public spending cuts, convertibility plan pegging currency to dollar. Initially, reforms controlled inflation, brought economic growth, but also caused unemployment, increased inequality and dependence on foreign capital. Menem amended constitution allowing re-election, elected again in 1995.

events.title: Military Government Leaders Pardoned
events.description: President Menem issued pardons releasing convicted military government leaders including Jorge Videla. Menem called pardons necessary step for 'national reconciliation,' but decision sparked anger from human rights organizations and victims' families. Pardons viewed as insult to justice and victims, marking continuation of impunity culture. Despite pardons, human rights organizations continued fighting, seeking other legal avenues to prosecute crimes.

events.title: AMIA Bombing
events.description: Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires hit by car bomb, killing 29, injuring 242. In 1994, Jewish community center (AMIA) hit by deadlier bombing, killing 85, injuring over 300. Investigation pointed to Iran and Hezbollah, but case filled with corruption and negligence, no one brought to justice to date. These attacks were Latin America's deadliest terrorist attacks, exposing serious problems in Argentine judicial system.

events.title: Unemployment and Social Crisis
events.description: Despite macroeconomic stability, Menem's neoliberal reforms caused massive unemployment (over 18%) and poverty. Privatization and de-industrialization made hundreds of thousands jobless. New social movements emerged, including unemployed workers movement (piqueteros), protesting unemployment and poverty through road blockades. Social inequality expanded dramatically, Argentina transformed from relatively equal society to highly unequal society.

events.title: Alliance Government Rises
events.description: Radical Party's Fernando de la Rúa elected president as center-left Alliance candidate, ending Peronist Party's ten-year rule. De la Rúa promised to fight corruption, restore ethics and transparency, but inherited serious economic problems: high foreign debt, economic recession, unemployment and convertibility plan's unsustainability. De la Rúa lacked political skills and congressional majority, making crisis response difficult.

events.title: Economic Collapse and Social Unrest
events.description: Argentina plunged into severe economic and political crisis. Government unable to pay foreign debt, IMF stopped loans, economy fell into deep recession. In December, government implemented 'Corralito' (deposit freeze), restricting people from withdrawing cash from banks, triggering massive protests. Middle class took to streets banging pots and pans (cacerolazo) protesting, poor neighborhoods looted supermarkets. Police repression caused about 30 deaths. December 20, President de la Rúa fled presidential palace by helicopter, resigning presidency. This was one of most severe crises in modern Argentine history.

events.title: Political Chaos and Default
events.description: After de la Rúa's resignation, Argentina went through five presidents in just two weeks. Finally, Senate President Eduardo Duhalde appointed interim president. Early 2002, Argentina declared default on about $100 billion foreign debt, then history's largest sovereign debt default. Government abandoned convertibility plan pegging to dollar, currency massively devalued. GDP fell nearly 11%, unemployment exceeded 20%, poverty exceeded 50%. This crisis destroyed middle class savings, triggered massive emigration wave.

events.title: Kirchner Elected President
events.description: Néstor Kirchner elected president with modest vote share (he got 22% in first round, but opponent Menem withdrew from second round). Kirchner represented Peronist left, promised to break with neoliberalism, rebuild state role, pursue social justice. He promoted debt restructuring (drastically cutting debt), reopened Dirty War cases, renewed Supreme Court, supported human rights. Kirchner's policies benefited from high commodity prices like soybeans in early 2000s, economy began recovering.

events.title: Amnesty Laws Abolished
events.description: Argentine Supreme Court declared 1980s amnesty laws unconstitutional, opening door for retrying Dirty War criminals. Kirchner government actively supported this decision, hundreds of former officers and police tried for human rights crimes. This was major victory for human rights movement, marking crucial step toward truth and justice. Argentina became one of Latin America's most progressive nations in prosecuting past crimes.

events.title: Cristina Fernández Elected President
events.description: Néstor Kirchner's wife Cristina Fernández de Kirchner (CFK) elected president, becoming Argentina's first elected female president (Isabel Perón became president through succession). Cristina continued husband's policies, expanding social programs, imposing high taxes on agricultural exports, promoting energy nationalization, allying with left-wing governments like Venezuela. Her style more charismatic and confrontational, engaging in fierce conflicts with media and agricultural sector.

events.title: Agricultural Crisis
events.description: Cristina government raised export taxes on soybeans and other agricultural products, triggering massive agricultural sector protests. Farmers blockaded roads for months, urban population divided supporting and opposing government. Finally, Senate Vice President Julio Cobos voted against government, causing proposal to fail. This conflict exposed deep divisions between urban-rural, pro and anti-Kirchnerism, weakening government authority.

events.title: Néstor Kirchner's Death
events.description: Former President Néstor Kirchner died of heart attack at age 60. His death triggered national mourning, hundreds of thousands attended funeral. Néstor viewed as leader who brought Argentina out of 2001 crisis, his death major blow to Cristina government, as he was key political operator behind scenes. This also marked beginning of Kirchner era's end.

events.title: Cristina Re-elected
events.description: Cristina Fernández re-elected with 54% vote share, highest since democracy restored. Her re-election reflected economic growth, social programs and sympathy votes after husband's death. However, second term faced increasing economic problems: inflation, currency controls, foreign exchange shortages, accusations of government statistics manipulation.

events.title: YPF Oil Company Nationalization
events.description: Cristina government nationalized Spanish Repsol-owned YPF oil company, claiming need to ensure energy sovereignty and address energy shortages. This decision welcomed by nationalists but triggered diplomatic crisis with Spain, scared away foreign investors, led to Argentina's greater international isolation. Nationalization also failed to solve energy problems, Argentina transformed from energy exporter to importer.

events.title: Debt Default and Vulture Funds
events.description: Argentina again fell into technical debt default due to legal dispute with 'vulture funds' (creditors refusing to participate in 2005 and 2010 debt restructurings). US court ruled Argentina must fully repay these creditors, but government refused, leading to inability to pay restructured creditors. This dispute led to Argentina's exclusion from international capital markets again, exacerbating economic difficulties.

events.title: Macri Elected President
events.description: Center-right candidate Mauricio Macri narrowly defeated Peronist candidate Daniel Scioli in runoff, ending 12 years of Kirchnerism. Macri promised to end currency controls, reintegrate with world economy, fight corruption, restore independent statistics. He represented change, attracting voters tired of inflation, corruption and confrontational politics. But he lacked congressional majority, faced strong Peronist opposition.

events.title: Vulture Funds Dispute Resolved
events.description: Macri government reached agreement with vulture funds, paying about $9.5 billion, ending 15-year legal dispute. This enabled Argentina to return to international capital markets, able to issue bonds for financing. But critics said government paid too much, yielded to speculators. Agreement marked Macri's effort to 'normalize' Argentina's relations with global financial system.

events.title: Currency Crisis and IMF Bailout
events.description: Argentine peso massively devalued, triggering new economic crisis. Investors lost confidence in Macri government's gradual reforms, capital fled, inflation soared. Macri forced to seek $57 billion bailout loan from IMF, IMF's largest loan in history. But loan came with strict austerity conditions, cutting public spending, intensifying recession. IMF had poor reputation in Argentine history (viewed as culprit in 2001 crisis), this decision extremely unpopular.

events.title: Fernández Elected President
events.description: Peronist Party's Alberto Fernández with Cristina Kirchner as vice presidential candidate won election, defeating Macri seeking re-election. Fernández promised to exit economic recession, ease IMF loan burden, restore social spending. He faced severe challenges: economic recession, 50% poverty rate, high inflation and massive foreign debt. His victory marked voters' rejection of Macri's neoliberal policies, but also reflected Kirchnerism's return.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Lockdown
events.description: Argentina implemented Latin America's strictest and longest lockdown measures responding to COVID-19 pandemic. Strict lockdown lasted months, severely hitting economy, GDP falling nearly 10%. Despite lockdown measures, Argentina became one of world's countries with highest per capita COVID-19 death rates. Pandemic exacerbated already severe economic and social crisis, poverty rate exceeding 40%, middle class continued shrinking.

events.title: Debt Restructuring
events.description: Fernández government reached agreement with private creditors, restructuring about $65 billion debt, obtaining debt relief and deferred payments. This was key to avoiding catastrophic default, but Argentina still faced debt negotiations with IMF. Restructuring showed Argentine debt unsustainable, but didn't solve fundamental economic problems.

events.title: Inflation Out of Control and Political Crisis
events.description: Argentine inflation rate exceeded 100%, people's purchasing power fell sharply. Peso continuously devalued, government implemented price controls and currency controls but couldn't control inflation. Alberto Fernández and Vice President Cristina's relationship publicly ruptured, ruling coalition fell into infighting. Cristina's supporters criticized president for weakness and incompetence, Fernández became lame duck, approval ratings plummeted. Economic and political crisis planted seeds for 2023 election.

events.title: Milei Elected President
events.description: Far-right libertarian Javier Milei upset defeated Peronist Party in election, elected president. Milei was political outsider, economist, known for radical rhetoric, promising to 'chainsaw' cut state, abolish central bank, dollarize economy, drastically cut public spending. His victory reflected voters' complete weariness with traditional parties and desperation over triple-digit inflation and continued economic decline. Milei's extreme libertarianism and eccentric personality (including keeping five cloned dogs) made him global focus. His election marked dramatic shift in Argentine politics, future full of uncertainty.

events.title: Milei's Shock Therapy
events.description: President Milei implemented radical economic reforms including drastically cutting public spending, removing price controls, massive currency devaluation, cutting subsidies, reducing government departments and civil servants. Reforms caused severe pain short-term: real wages fell, poverty rate exceeded 50%, economic activity contracted. But inflation began declining, fiscal deficit turned to surplus. Milei's reforms extremely controversial, triggering massive protests, but he maintained hardline stance. He openly confronted leftists, unions, human rights organizations and traditional politicians, calling himself 'freedom fighter' against 'political parasite class.' Argentina again at crossroads of economic and social experimentation, results will determine nation's direction for coming decades. Milei's presidency is latest chapter in Argentina's cyclical crises and radical policy swings, this once-wealthy nation continues searching for path to stability and prosperity.
